newsitem.title: UK: Rushdie slams EU for its dealings with Iran.
newsitem.headline: Rushdie slams EU for its dealings with Iran.

text.p: British author Salman Rushdie has criticised the European Union for its inability to persuade Iran to lift its death threat against him and accused Islamic extremists of attacking intellectual freedom.

Nearly eight years after Iran's late spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini imposed a death threat, or fatwa, on Rushdie for allegedly blaspheming Islam in his novel "The Satanic Verses", the India-born writer is still a hunted man.
His movements are less restricted than they were and he says he does not spend his days thinking he is going to be killed.
But he still lives in hiding and is disappointed that the European Union and the international community have not done more to pressure Iran to lift the fatwa.

"What I would have liked to have happened was that the maximum pressure was applied to the people that issued the threat and a greater effort was made to remove the threat from the people who are targeted," he said in an interview ahead of the anniversary of the imposition of the fatwa on February 14.
"Sometimes I think the opposite has happened," he told Reuters Television.

Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera last month that twice Tehran had come close to a deal with the EU to resolve the Rushdie affair, but on both occassions a settlement had been blocked by one country. He strongly hinted that Britain was the culprit.
Iran maintains that the fatwa against Rushdie is irrevocable but says it will not send anyone to kill the author.
Britain's official line is that it will maintain pressure on Iran to lift the death threat and to assure the author's safety.
"The critical dialogue with Iran...has achieved absolutely nothing," Rushdie said.

"It makes me feel it is a very useful fig leaf for the European Union. They can claim to be doing something about human rights in Iran while actually many European states are trying to increase their trade relations (with Iran)."

Despite the fatwa Rushdie has managed to gradually increase his public appearances and has travelled abroad to accept literary awards. He believes the threat against him is symptomatic of what is going on elsewhere in the world, particularly in Iran, Algeria, Egypt, India and Pakistan.

"There has been a concerted attack on intellectual freedom by Islamic extremists in these countries. It is a worldwide tragedy," he said, adding that he was lucky not to be in the country where the repression was taking place.
Despite the persecution and uncertainty he has had to live with, Rushdie has no regrets about writing "The Satanic Verses", only about what has happened to the work.
His next novel, which he is currently working on, will be about something completely different -- rock 'n' roll.
"It is one of the few phenomena of our times that has crossed every frontier in the world," he said.
